The pass-1 activations hold, for each of 512 DEV problems and every layer, the residual at the last prompt token and the residual averaged over the answer's tokens. That is what I need: the mean answer-token state serves as a typical answer query.

I build each layer's queries from it and apply the query/key norms. For each group, I build keys from the mean input at the final prompt token in the prompt-only pass. For every layer and head I then measure how many logits more strongly the end-of-prompt key attracts the typical answer query on math than on poem prompts. I compare G1 with G5 (same instruction) and G2 with G3 (no instruction).

RoPE rotates the query–key product with distance, so I compute this two ways:
- all dimensions, with rotation ignored;
- only the slowly rotating dimensions (wavelength over 2,000 tokens), which keep their alignment at answer distances.

I also measure how much the end-of-prompt key stands out above the other shared tail positions in the math group.

If L18's heads attract the answer queries several logits more on math than any other layer does, L18's key outlier is an attention diverter and a lead for a causal test. If its numbers sit inside the range of the other layers, the outlier is ordinary task routing and I close it.

The key-side outlier is not a diverter. L18's heads attract a typical answer query only 0.5–0.9 logits more on math than on poem prompts. That is inside the normal range: the median over all layers and heads is 0.2–0.3 and the 90th percentile about 1.0.

The largest math-conditional attraction is at L11 head 2: 2.6 logits without the instruction, 1.7 with it. That is the known broadcast head whose v̂ content V1 already removes. L12–13 heads follow at 1.4–2.1 logits, but their value projections have ordinary gains, so they read the task state naturally. I close the key side.

The search for a second plant has now covered:
- values at every trailing prompt position and every layer;
- keys;
- MLP units, norms and spectra.

Nothing beyond L11's value amplifier turned up. V1 stays the edit.

With 14 passes left and no new candidate, I complete the causal evidence for V1. Its dose curve so far covers only removal (strength 0 → 0, 0.5 → +6.3, 1 → +25.4 on DEV[0:256]). If the v̂ broadcast really is a brake, doubling it (strength −1) should push accuracy below the original's on the same problems. No change would mean the switch is already saturated in the original.

In this block I first check that the direction is stable:
- the two halves of DEV[:512] should give the same direction;
- an independent teacher-forced prompt set should match too.

I also verify on summary vectors that the amplification doubles the math end-of-prompt value. I then save it as a temporary test edit (not a candidate) and log the planned pass. V1 stays safe in `/work/best_V1` and will be restored right after.

The direction is completely stable. The two halves of DEV[:512] give the same direction as the saved v̂ (cosine 1.0000 each), and so do the teacher-forced math prompts. Those prompts overlap with DEV[:512], so the last check is not independent, but the halves alone show the point: the end-of-prompt value at L11 is a task state, essentially the same for every math problem, not something problem-specific.

The amplification test edit A1 is saved and behaves as planned on summary vectors. The math end-of-prompt value along v̂ doubles from 16 to 32, and ordinary tokens double too (for example 1.09 → 2.18).

I now run the original and A1 on DEV[0:256], the same slice as the removal points of the dose curve:

| Strength | Paired gain on DEV[0:256] |
|---|---|
| 0 (original) | 0 |
| 0.5 | +6.3 |
| 1 (V1) | +25.4 |
| −1 (A1, this pass) | ? |

If the broadcast is a brake that scales with its size, A1 should land below the original: a negative paired difference, likely with more answers cut at the token limit. A difference near zero would mean the original's switch already does its full damage at 16 units. A positive difference would contradict the brake reading.

Doubling the broadcast hurt, as predicted:
- Accuracy fell from 22.3% to 13.7% on the same 256 problems (−8.6 ± 2.4 points: 30 right→wrong against 8 wrong→right).
- Answers cut at the token limit rose from 23% to 39%, and answers grew by about 100 tokens.

With the earlier removal points, the same-slice dose curve is monotone:

| Strength | Paired gain on DEV[0:256] |
|---|---|
| −1 (doubled) | −8.6 |
| 0 (original) | 0 |
| 0.5 | +6.3 |
| 1 (V1, removed) | +25.4 |

The size of the v̂ broadcast controls math accuracy in both directions, so it is a brake. Its effect is steepest near zero, where even a small leftover still does much of the harm. This is the causal evidence the method asks for, at several strengths.

One question about the strength remains: is the best point exactly at removal? If the harm depends only on the size of the broadcast, over-removal should be worse than V1. I test strength 1.25, which leaves −4 units at the math end-of-prompt and about −0.2 at ordinary tokens. If the harm depends on the signed value, pushing slightly past zero could help.

One pass on the same slice decides. I would pursue 1.25 further only if it beats V1's +25.4 there by a clear margin (about 6 points or more, given the churn I measured between similar edits). Otherwise V1 stays.
